# Adaptive Control System for Pressure Support Ventilation Based on Work/Power of Breathing Estimation

## System Overview

Mechanical ventilators supporting patients with impaired respiratory function often employ pressure support ventilation (PSV) as a mode of assisted breathing, wherein the ventilator supplements the patient's spontaneous inspiratory effort with a controlled level of positive airway pressure. To optimize this support and ensure it is appropriately matched to the patient's physiological needs, a closed-loop control architecture can be implemented that continuously monitors and adjusts the level of pressure assistance delivered. This document describes such a system, which incorporates real-time estimation of the patient's respiratory effort, feedback-based error correction, and adaptive control parameter tuning to maintain both therapeutic efficacy and system stability.

## Power of Breathing / Work of Breathing Estimation

At the core of the control system is a power of breathing (PoB) or work of breathing (WoB) estimator, which continuously monitors relevant physiological and mechanical signals—such as airway pressure, flow, and volume—to derive a real-time estimate of the respiratory effort being exerted by the patient. This estimator processes the sensor data to generate a corresponding PoB or WoB signal, which serves as a quantitative representation of how much work the patient is performing to breathe under the current level of ventilatory support. This signal is critical to the overall control strategy, as it provides the feedback variable necessary to determine whether the current pressure support setting is adequately reducing the patient's breathing burden, or whether adjustment is required.

## Error Signal Generation

The estimated PoB or WoB signal is subsequently compared against a predetermined set point value, which represents the clinician-specified or system-determined target level of patient respiratory effort. This comparison is performed by an error calculator, which computes the difference between the real-time estimated signal and the set point, thereby producing an error signal. This error signal reflects the deviation between the patient's actual work of breathing and the desired target, and it serves as the primary input driving the subsequent control action. A positive or negative error indicates whether the patient is working harder or easier than the target level, respectively, and the magnitude of the error indicates the degree of deviation from the desired operating point.

## Controller and PSV Signal Generation

The error signal generated by the error calculator is fed into a controller, which applies its transfer function to the error signal in order to generate an appropriate control action. Specifically, the controller multiplies the error signal by its transfer function—which may be implemented using classical control strategies such as proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control, or more advanced model-based control techniques—to produce a PSV control signal. This PSV control signal is then transmitted to the mechanical ventilator, where it dictates the level of pressure support to be delivered to the patient during each inspiratory cycle. Through this closed-loop feedback mechanism, the system continuously adjusts the pressure support level in an effort to drive the patient's estimated PoB or WoB toward the desired set point.

## Patient Adaptation and Model Fitting

Because patient respiratory mechanics and effort characteristics can vary significantly between individuals, and may also change over time due to factors such as fatigue, changes in respiratory drive, or evolving lung mechanics, the control system incorporates a patient adaptation component designed to personalize and continuously refine the control strategy. This adaptation component operates by collecting data pertaining to both the PoB or WoB signal and the PSV control signal during ongoing closed-loop operation of the ventilator. Using this collected data, the adaptation component fits the parameters of a model that represents the dynamics of the controlled ventilation system—that is, it identifies a mathematical representation of how the patient's respiratory effort responds to changes in the level of pressure support provided.

This model-fitting process may employ system identification techniques, recursive parameter estimation, or other adaptive algorithms capable of updating model parameters based on streaming input-output data collected during actual patient use. The resulting patient-specific model captures the unique respiratory response characteristics of the individual being ventilated, accounting for factors such as lung compliance, airway resistance, and the patient's own respiratory muscle effort dynamics.

## Real-Time Controller Adaptation for Stability

Based on the parameters derived from this patient-specific model, the adaptation component dynamically adjusts the parameters of the controller's transfer function in real time. This continuous adjustment ensures that the controller's response characteristics remain appropriately matched to the current dynamics of the patient-ventilator system, even as those dynamics evolve over the course of treatment. By tailoring the controller parameters to reflect the identified patient model, the adaptation component helps to ensure that the closed-loop system remains stable, avoiding issues such as oscillatory pressure delivery, overshoot, or sluggish response that could otherwise arise from a mismatch between a fixed, generic controller design and the specific, time-varying characteristics of the individual patient.

## Summary

Taken together, these components form an integrated adaptive control system for pressure support ventilation. The PoB/WoB estimator provides continuous feedback on patient respiratory effort; the error calculator quantifies the deviation from a desired target; the controller translates this error into an actionable PSV control signal; and the patient adaptation component ensures that the underlying control parameters remain appropriately tuned to the specific and evolving characteristics of the patient. This architecture enables the ventilator to deliver personalized, responsive, and stable respiratory support, thereby helping to optimize patient comfort, reduce the risk of over- or under-assistance, and improve overall ventilatory management.

# Mechanical Ventilator System with Adaptive Pressure Support Ventilation Control

## Background

Mechanical ventilation systems are widely used in clinical settings to provide respiratory support to patients who are unable to breathe adequately on their own. One common mode of ventilatory support is Pressure Support Ventilation (PSV), wherein the ventilator delivers a preset level of positive pressure during spontaneous inspiratory efforts to reduce the patient's work of breathing while preserving the patient's own respiratory drive and control over breath timing, depth, and flow.

A significant challenge in PSV management is determining the appropriate level of pressure support for an individual patient. Insufficient support can lead to excessive patient effort, respiratory muscle fatigue, and delayed weaning, while excessive support can cause over-assistance, muscle deconditioning, and patient-ventilator asynchrony. Traditional approaches to PSV titration often rely on intermittent clinical assessments, static settings, or manual adjustments by clinicians, which may not adequately respond to a patient's changing respiratory status or effort levels in real time.

## Summary of the Invention

The present disclosure provides a mechanical ventilator system configured to address these challenges through closed-loop, patient-adaptive control of pressure support ventilation. The system comprises a Power of Breathing/Work of Breathing (PoB/WoB) estimator configured to continuously or periodically estimate the patient's respiratory effort based on measured or derived physiological signals, such as airway pressure, flow, and volume. The PoB/WoB estimator generates a feedback signal representative of the patient's current work of breathing or power of breathing.

This feedback signal is provided to an error calculator, which compares the estimated PoB/WoB feedback signal to a predetermined or clinician-specified set point representing a target level of patient effort. The error calculator generates an error signal indicative of the deviation between the actual and desired respiratory effort.

A controller receives the error signal and adjusts the pressure support ventilation parameters—such as the pressure support level, rise time, or cycling criteria—in order to drive the error signal toward zero, thereby maintaining the patient's work of breathing at or near the desired set point. The controller may be implemented using any suitable control architecture, including but not limited to proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control, model predictive control (MPC), or other feedback control methodologies known in the art.

## Patient Adaptation Component

A key aspect of the disclosed system is the inclusion of a patient adaptation component configured to enhance the performance and robustness of the closed-loop control system by dynamically identifying and fitting patient-specific model parameters. Because individual patients exhibit significant variability in respiratory mechanics—including differences in lung compliance, airway resistance, and respiratory muscle strength—a fixed or generic controller transfer function may not provide optimal or stable performance across all patients or across changing conditions in a single patient over time.

To address this variability, the patient adaptation component receives real-time data comprising the PoB/WoB feedback signal and the control signal(s) generated by the controller. Using this data, the patient adaptation component performs system identification or parameter estimation techniques to fit a patient-specific model that characterizes the relationship between the applied pressure support control inputs and the resulting patient respiratory effort outputs. Suitable techniques for this parameter fitting may include recursive least squares estimation, Kalman filtering, gradient-based optimization, or other adaptive estimation algorithms known in the art.

Based on the dynamically fitted patient-specific model parameters, the patient adaptation component continuously or periodically updates the transfer function employed by the controller. This adaptive updating ensures that the controller's response characteristics remain matched to the current respiratory mechanics and effort patterns of the individual patient, even as those characteristics change over time due to factors such as disease progression, sedation level, fatigue, or recovery.

By continuously adjusting the controller's transfer function in this manner, the system maintains closed-loop stability despite variations in patient physiology, and avoids the performance degradation or instability that might otherwise occur if a static controller design were used across diverse or changing patient conditions.

## Advantages

The disclosed mechanical ventilator system provides several advantages over conventional PSV control approaches. First, by employing real-time PoB/WoB estimation and closed-loop error correction, the system enables continuous, automated titration of pressure support levels, reducing the need for frequent manual adjustments by clinical staff. Second, the patient adaptation component enables personalized ventilatory support that is tailored to the specific and evolving respiratory characteristics of each patient, potentially improving patient comfort, reducing the risk of ventilator-induced diaphragmatic dysfunction, and facilitating more effective weaning from mechanical ventilation. Third, the dynamic model-fitting approach helps ensure robust closed-loop stability, reducing the risk of oscillatory or unstable ventilator behavior that could otherwise arise from patient-to-patient variability or intra-patient changes over the course of treatment.

## Exemplary Implementation

In an exemplary embodiment, the PoB/WoB estimator may compute the estimated work of breathing using a pressure-volume or pressure-time product methodology based on measured airway pressure and estimated or measured patient effort signals (e.g., esophageal pressure, when available, or surrogate measures derived from airway pressure and flow waveforms). The set point for the error calculator may be established by a clinician based on desired therapeutic goals (e.g., targeting a specific work of breathing range associated with reduced risk of both over-assistance and under-assistance) or may be automatically determined based on patient-specific baseline measurements.

The controller may output a pressure support level command that is transmitted to the ventilator's pneumatic control system, which regulates the delivery of pressurized gas to the patient in accordance with the commanded pressure support level. Concurrently, the patient adaptation component may operate in the background, continuously refining its estimate of the patient-specific model parameters using techniques such as recursive parameter estimation, and periodically or continuously updating the controller's transfer function coefficients accordingly.

This adaptive architecture allows the mechanical ventilator system to provide safe, effective, and personalized pressure support ventilation that adjusts in real time to the unique and changing respiratory needs of each individual patient, thereby improving clinical outcomes and reducing the burden on clinical staff associated with manual ventilator management.

# Key Terms in Offshore Oil & Gas Operations: PSV, PoB, and WoB

In the offshore oil and gas industry, a range of specialized acronyms are used daily to describe vessels, safety protocols, and drilling operations. Three of the most commonly referenced terms are PSV, PoB, and WoB.

## PSV (Platform Supply Vessel)

A Platform Supply Vessel is a specially designed ship used to transport supplies, equipment, and materials to and from offshore oil and gas platforms. These vessels are essential for maintaining continuous operations on rigs that are often located far from shore. PSVs typically carry cargo such as drilling fluids, cement, fuel, water, food, and spare parts. They are engineered with dynamic positioning systems, allowing them to maintain precise location alongside platforms even in rough sea conditions, which is critical for safe cargo transfer operations.

## PoB (Persons on Board)

PoB refers to the total number of people present on an offshore installation or vessel at any given time. This figure is one of the most critical pieces of safety information in the industry, as it must be accurately tracked and readily available in case of an emergency evacuation, search and rescue operation, or incident investigation. Offshore installation managers are required to maintain up-to-date PoB records, and this number is regularly communicated to onshore emergency response teams and regulatory bodies to ensure compliance with safety standards.

## WoB (Weight on Bit)

Weight on Bit is a key drilling parameter that refers to the amount of downward force applied to the drill bit during drilling operations. This measurement directly influences the rate of penetration into the rock formation and affects overall drilling efficiency. Drillers must carefully monitor and adjust WoB to optimize performance while avoiding excessive wear on the drill bit or damage to the drill string. Too little weight can result in slow progress, while too much can cause premature bit failure or drilling problems such as bit whirl or vibration.

## Conclusion

Together, PSV, PoB, and WoB represent just a small sample of the technical vocabulary used in offshore drilling and production operations. Understanding these terms is essential for anyone working in or studying the oil and gas sector, as they touch on logistics, safety management, and technical drilling performance—three pillars that underpin successful and safe offshore operations.

# TECHNICAL DESCRIPTION

## CLOSED-LOOP MECHANICAL VENTILATION SYSTEM WITH AUTOMATED PRESSURE SUPPORT ADJUSTMENT BASED ON PATIENT WORK OF BREATHING

---

### FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure relates to mechanical ventilation systems, and more particularly to a closed-loop ventilator apparatus and method for automatically titrating inspiratory pressure support based on real-time estimation of patient respiratory work of breathing (WOB), thereby maintaining a target level of patient respiratory effort while minimizing both over-assistance and under-assistance during mechanical ventilation.

---

### BACKGROUND

Mechanical ventilators provide respiratory support to patients unable to sustain adequate spontaneous ventilation. In pressure support ventilation (PSV) modes, clinicians manually set an inspiratory pressure level intended to reduce the patient's work of breathing to a comfortable range. However, static pressure settings do not account for dynamic changes in patient respiratory drive, lung mechanics (compliance and resistance), or disease progression. Consequently, patients may experience:

- **Over-assistance**, leading to muscle atrophy, patient-ventilator asynchrony, and prolonged weaning; or
- **Under-assistance**, causing excessive respiratory muscle fatigue, dyspnea, and risk of ventilatory failure.

Existing closed-loop systems (e.g., Proportional Assist Ventilation, Neurally Adjusted Ventilatory Assist) attempt to address this but typically require specialized sensors (e.g., esophageal balloon catheters or diaphragmatic EMG electrodes) that are invasive, costly, or not universally available. There exists a need for a system that estimates WOB using non-invasive or minimally invasive signals and automatically adjusts pressure support in a stable, clinically safe manner.

---

### SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

Disclosed herein is a closed-loop mechanical ventilation system comprising:

1. A **sensor subsystem** configured to acquire real-time airway pressure, flow, and volume signals, and optionally surface diaphragmatic electromyography (EMGdi) or esophageal pressure signals;
2. A **work-of-breathing estimation module** configured to compute an instantaneous and trended patient WOB metric using a computational model that decomposes total work into patient-generated and ventilator-generated components;
3. A **controller module** implementing a feedback control algorithm (e.g., PID, fuzzy logic, or model-predictive control) that compares estimated WOB to a clinician-defined target range and generates a corrective pressure support adjustment signal;
4. A **pressure delivery subsystem** that modulates inspiratory pressure in real time according to the controller output, subject to safety-bounded rate limits and absolute pressure ceilings/floors;
5. A **safety and alarm subsystem** that monitors for signal degradation, apnea, leak, or asynchrony events and reverts to a preset backup ventilation mode when necessary.

The system continuously adjusts pressure support breath-by-breath or over rolling windows of multiple breaths, maintaining patient WOB within a physiologically appropriate target (e.g., 0.3–0.7 Joules/liter), thereby reducing the risks associated with static pressure support settings.

---

### DETAILED DESCRIPTION

#### 1. System Architecture

Referring to the accompanying schematic (FIG. 1), the ventilator system (100) comprises a gas delivery unit (110), a patient interface (120) (e.g., endotracheal tube or non-invasive mask), an integrated sensor array (130), a signal processing unit (140), a WOB estimation module (150), a closed-loop controller (160), and a user interface/display (170).

**Gas Delivery Unit (110):** Includes a blower or turbine, proportional flow control valve, oxygen blending module, and pressure transducer, enabling breath-by-breath modulation of inspiratory pressure (PSV level), rise time, and cycling threshold.

**Sensor Array (130):** Comprises:
- Proximal airway pressure transducer (Paw)
- Pneumotachograph or hot-wire flow sensor (measuring flow, Q)
- Volume integration derived from flow
- Optional esophageal pressure catheter (Pes) for direct pleural pressure surrogate
- Optional surface EMGdi electrodes positioned parasternally or at the costal margin
- Optional accessory muscle activity sensor (e.g., sternocleidomastoid EMG) for non-invasive effort estimation

#### 2. Work of Breathing Estimation Module (150)

The WOB module computes patient work of breathing using one or more of the following methods, selectable based on available sensor configuration:

**(a) Campbell Diagram Method (Invasive):**
Using esophageal pressure and volume signals, the module computes the area between the dynamic chest wall compliance line and the actual pressure-volume loop during inspiration:

```
WOB_patient = ∫ Pmus × dV
```

where Pmus (patient respiratory muscle pressure) is derived as:

```
Pmus(t) = Pes(t) − Pcw(t)
```

with Pcw representing the passive chest wall recoil pressure estimated from patient-specific compliance.

**(b) Non-Invasive Estimation Method:**
In the absence of esophageal catheterization, the module estimates Pmus using a parameter-adaptive respiratory system model:

```
Paw(t) + Pmus(t) = (V(t)/C) + (Q(t) × R) + PEEP
```

where:
- Paw = airway pressure (measured)
- V = volume (measured)
- Q = flow (measured)
- C = respiratory system compliance (estimated via recursive least squares or Kalman filtering during passive/controlled breaths)
- R = airway resistance (similarly estimated)

Solving for Pmus:

```
Pmus(t) = (V(t)/C) + (Q(t) × R) + PEEP − Paw(t)
```

The instantaneous WOB is then computed as:

```
WOB_patient = ∫ Pmus(t) × Q(t) dt   [over inspiratory phase]
```

normalized to tidal volume to yield WOB in Joules/liter.

**(c) EMG-Based Neuro-Mechanical Index:**
Where surface EMGdi is available, a neuro-mechanical efficiency index correlates integrated EMG amplitude with Pmus, providing a redundant or primary estimate, particularly useful when compliance/resistance estimation is unreliable (e.g., in the presence of intrinsic PEEP or active expiration).

**(d) Sensor Fusion:**
A Kalman filter or weighted-average fusion algorithm combines estimates from methods (a)–(c) when multiple signal sources are available, improving robustness and reducing estimation variance.

#### 3. Closed-Loop Controller (160)

The controller receives the trended WOB signal (e.g., a moving average over N=3–5 breaths to reduce breath-to-breath noise) and compares it to a clinician-set target WOB range (WOB_target ± tolerance).

**Control Law (example — PID implementation):**

```
ΔPS(t) = Kp × e(t) + Ki × ∫e(t)dt + Kd × (de(t)/dt)
```

where:
- e(t) = WOB_measured(t) − WOB_target
- Kp, Ki, Kd = tunable gains (patient-population-specific defaults, clinician-adjustable)
- ΔPS(t) = incremental adjustment to pressure support level

**Constraint Logic:**
The output pressure support level (PS_new = PS_current + ΔPS) is bounded by:

```
PS_min ≤ PS_new ≤ PS_max
|ΔPS per adjustment interval| ≤ ΔPS_max_rate
```

Adjustment intervals are configurable (e.g., every 30–60 seconds, or every N breaths) to avoid oscillatory hunting and to allow patient respiratory pattern stabilization between changes.

**Alternative Control Strategies:**
- **Fuzzy Logic Controller:** Employs rule-based inference (e.g., "IF WOB is High AND trend is Increasing THEN increase PS by Medium increment") for smoother handling of nonlinear patient responses.
- **Model Predictive Control (MPC):** Uses a patient-specific respiratory mechanics model to predict future WOB trajectories and optimize pressure support trajectory over a receding horizon, subject to safety constraints.

#### 4. Safety and Alarm Subsystem

The system incorporates multiple safety layers:

- **Signal Validity Monitor:** Continuously assesses signal-to-noise ratio, sensor disconnection, or physiologically implausible values; triggers fallback to last known-good PS setting or clinician-set backup mode.
- **Asynchrony Detector:** Identifies ineffective triggering, double-triggering, or flow asynchrony using flow/pressure waveform pattern recognition; suspends automated adjustment and alerts clinician if asynchrony index exceeds threshold.
- **Apnea/Backup Ventilation:** Reverts to mandatory backup ventilation (e.g., pressure control or volume control) if no patient trigger is detected within a configurable timeout window.
- **Rate-of-Change Limiting:** Prevents abrupt pressure support changes that could destabilize patient breathing pattern.
- **Clinician Override:** All automated adjustments remain visible and reversible via the user interface; manual override at any time disables closed-loop control and reverts to standard PSV.

#### 5. User Interface (170)

The interface displays:
- Real-time WOB trend graph with target range overlay
- Current and historical pressure support levels
- Sensor status indicators
- Adjustable target WOB range and controller gain parameters
- Event log of automated adjustments and rationale (for auditability)

---

### EXEMPLARY OPERATIONAL SEQUENCE (FIG. 2)

1. Ventilator initiates in standard PSV mode with clinician-set baseline pressure support.
2. Sensor array acquires Paw, Q, V (and optionally Pes/EMGdi) continuously.
3. Signal processing unit filters and synchronizes signals to breath phase (inspiration/expiration boundaries detected via flow zero-crossing or trigger algorithm).
4. WOB estimation module computes per-breath WOB using selected method(s).
5. Rolling average WOB is compared against target range by controller module.
6. If WOB is outside target range for a sustained period (e.g., 3 consecutive breaths), controller computes ΔPS and issues command to gas delivery unit.
7. Gas delivery unit adjusts inspiratory pressure support within safety bounds.
8. System logs adjustment, updates display, and continues monitoring.
9. Safety subsystem continuously runs in parallel, capable of interrupting steps 6–7 upon detection of anomalous conditions.

---

### CLAIMS (ILLUSTRATIVE)

**Claim 1.** A closed-loop mechanical ventilation system comprising: a sensor subsystem configured to measure airway pressure, flow, and volume of a patient; a work-of-breathing estimation module configured to compute an estimate of patient-generated respiratory work of breathing from said measured signals using a respiratory system model incorporating estimated compliance and resistance parameters; a controller configured to compare said estimated work of breathing to a target range and to generate an adjustment signal for inspiratory pressure support; and a gas delivery subsystem configured to modulate inspiratory pressure support in response to said adjustment signal, subject to predefined safety limits on adjustment rate and absolute pressure bounds.

# Abstract

A ventilator control system and method are disclosed for automatically titrating pressure support ventilation (PSV) settings based on real-time patient work of breathing feedback. The system continuously calculates or estimates the patient's power of breathing (POB) from monitored respiratory parameters, including airway pressure, flow, and volume waveforms acquired during mechanical ventilation. A controller compares the calculated POB against a clinician-defined target range representing an optimal balance between ventilator-delivered support and patient respiratory muscle effort, avoiding both over-assistance (which promotes muscle atrophy and delayed weaning) and under-assistance (which causes patient fatigue and distress).

Based on the deviation between measured and target POB, the controller automatically adjusts one or more PSV parameters—including inspiratory pressure level, pressure rise time, inspiratory trigger sensitivity, and expiratory cycling threshold—using a closed-loop feedback algorithm. The algorithm may incorporate proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control, fuzzy logic, or model-based predictive control to ensure smooth, clinically safe adjustments while preventing oscillatory or abrupt changes in ventilator support. Safety limits, alarm thresholds, and rate-of-change constraints are incorporated to maintain adjustments within clinician-prescribed bounds.

The system further supports trending and logging of POB and corresponding ventilator settings over time, enabling automated or clinician-assisted weaning protocols in which pressure support is progressively reduced as patient respiratory capacity improves. Optional integration with additional physiological signals—such as respiratory rate, tidal volume, esophageal pressure, or diaphragmatic electrical activity—enhances the accuracy of POB estimation and enables the system to adapt to varying patient conditions and disease states.

By automating the continuous adjustment of PSV parameters in response to real-time patient effort, the invention reduces clinician workload, minimizes the risk of ventilator-induced diaphragmatic dysfunction, promotes patient-ventilator synchrony, and may accelerate the weaning process, thereby improving patient outcomes and reducing the duration of mechanical ventilation.

# PATENT APPLICATION LANGUAGE

## FIELD OF THE INVENTION

The present invention relates generally to mechanical ventilation systems, and more particularly to a mechanical ventilator system employing a work of breathing estimator in cooperation with an adaptive controller to maintain closed-loop stability during pressure support ventilation modes.

---

## BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

[0001] Mechanical ventilators provide respiratory assistance to patients experiencing inadequate spontaneous ventilation. In pressure support ventilation (PSV) modes, the ventilator delivers a clinician-set or automatically adjusted level of positive pressure during a patient-triggered inspiratory phase, thereby augmenting the patient's own respiratory effort. A persistent challenge in such systems is maintaining an appropriate balance between machine-delivered work and patient-generated work, particularly as patient respiratory mechanics, effort, and neural drive vary over time due to disease progression, sedation level, fatigue, or other physiological factors.

[0002] Conventional pressure support systems typically rely on fixed or manually-adjusted pressure support levels, which may result in either over-assistance (leading to respiratory muscle atrophy, patient-ventilator asynchrony, or delayed weaning) or under-assistance (leading to increased work of breathing, patient distress, and respiratory muscle fatigue). Existing closed-loop systems that attempt to automatically titrate pressure support often suffer from instability, oscillatory behavior, or delayed convergence when patient effort or mechanics change abruptly, due in part to inaccurate or noisy estimates of patient-contributed work of breathing and inadequately designed control architectures.

[0003] There exists a need for a ventilator system capable of accurately estimating patient work of breathing in real time and adaptively adjusting ventilatory support in a manner that preserves closed-loop stability across a range of patient conditions and disturbances.

---

## SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

[0004] The present invention addresses the foregoing needs by providing a mechanical ventilator system comprising a pneumatic delivery subsystem, a plurality of sensors, a work of breathing (WOB) estimator module, and an adaptive controller configured to adjust one or more pressure support parameters based on the estimated work of breathing while maintaining provable or empirically-verified closed-loop stability margins.

[0005] In one aspect, the WOB estimator module receives, as inputs, real-time measurements of airway pressure, flow, and volume, and optionally an estimate of respiratory muscle pressure (Pmus) derived from a respiratory system model, to compute an estimate of the work performed by the patient's respiratory muscles per breath or per unit time.

[0006] In another aspect, the adaptive controller receives the estimated work of breathing as a feedback signal and adjusts the pressure support level, rise time, cycling threshold, or other ventilatory parameters according to a control law having bounded gain adaptation rates, thereby preventing instability that could otherwise arise from rapid or unbounded parameter changes.

[0007] In a further aspect, the adaptive controller incorporates a stability-preserving mechanism, such as a Lyapunov-based adaptation law, a gain-scheduled proportional-integral-derivative (PID) structure with anti-windup, or a model reference adaptive control (MRAC) architecture with a projection operator constraining parameter estimates to a bounded set, so as to ensure that the closed-loop system remains stable notwithstanding variations in patient respiratory mechanics or effort.

---

## DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION

### System Overview

[0008] Referring now to FIG. 1, a mechanical ventilator system 100 is shown comprising a gas delivery module 110, a patient interface 120 (e.g., an endotracheal tube or mask), a sensor suite 130, a work of breathing estimator 140, an adaptive controller 150, and a central processing unit 160 configured to execute instructions stored in a non-transitory computer-readable medium 170.

[0009] The sensor suite 130 may include, without limitation, a flow sensor 131, an airway pressure sensor 132, a volume sensor (or integrator) 133, and, in certain embodiments, an esophageal balloon catheter or diaphragmatic electromyography (EMGdi) sensor 134 for direct or indirect estimation of respiratory muscle pressure.

### Work of Breathing Estimator

[0010] In an exemplary embodiment, the work of breathing estimator 140 computes an estimate of patient work of breathing (WOB_est) using a single-compartment respiratory system model expressed as:

$$P_{aw}(t) + P_{mus}(t) = R \cdot \dot{V}(t) + \frac{1}{C} \cdot V(t) + P_0$$

wherein P_aw(t) is measured airway pressure, P_mus(t) is the estimated or measured respiratory muscle pressure, R is patient airway resistance, C is respiratory system compliance, V̇(t) is flow, V(t) is volume, and P_0 is an offset term (e.g., PEEP).

[0011] In embodiments lacking direct P_mus measurement, the work of breathing estimator 140 may derive P_mus(t) using a recursive least-squares (RLS) or Kalman filter-based parameter estimation technique that jointly estimates R, C, and P_mus(t) from the measured P_aw(t), V̇(t), and V(t) signals, optionally constrained by known bounds on physiologically plausible parameter ranges.

[0012] The estimator 140 then computes an estimate of work of breathing per breath according to:

$$WOB_{est} = \int P_{mus}(t) \, dV(t)$$

integrated over the inspiratory phase, or, in alternative embodiments, using a proxy metric such as the pressure-time product (PTP) or an index derived from the derivative of P_mus(t).

[0013] It will be appreciated by one of ordinary skill in the art that the work of breathing estimator 140 may employ any of a plurality of estimation techniques, including but not limited to model-based estimation, machine learning-based regression (e.g., neural network or Gaussian process regression trained on historical patient data), or hybrid model/data-driven approaches, without departing from the scope of the invention.

### Adaptive Controller

[0014] The adaptive controller 150 is configured to receive the estimated work of breathing WOB_est(k) at each breath index k, compare it to a target work of breathing range [WOB_min, WOB_max] established by clinician input or a physiological reference model, and generate a control signal ΔP_support(k) representing an adjustment to the pressure support level.

[0015] In one embodiment, the adaptive controller 150 implements an update law of the form:

$$P_{support}(k+1) = P_{support}(k) + \gamma \cdot e(k)$$

wherein e(k) = WOB_target − WOB_est(k) is the work of breathing error at breath k, and γ is an adaptation gain selected to satisfy a stability criterion such that the closed-loop system exhibits bounded-input bounded-output (BIBO) stability notwithstanding bounded disturbances in patient effort or respiratory mechanics.

[0016] In a further embodiment, the adaptation gain γ is itself dynamically modulated according to a normalization function, for example:

$$\gamma(k) = \frac{\gamma_0}{1 + \|\phi(k)\|^2}$$

wherein φ(k) is a regressor vector comprising estimated patient mechanics parameters, and γ_0 is a base adaptation rate, such that the adaptation rate decreases in regions of high regressor magnitude to prevent parameter drift or instability—a technique sometimes referred to as normalized gradient adaptation.

[0017] In yet a further embodiment, the adaptive controller 150 employs a projection operator Proj{·} constraining the pressure support parameter estimate to remain within a predetermined safe operating envelope [P_min, P_max], such that:

$$P_{support}(k+1) = Proj\{P_{support}(k) + \gamma(k) \cdot e(k)\}$$

thereby ensuring that, even in the presence of estimation error or transient instability in the WOB estimator 140, the commanded pressure support level remains within clinically safe bounds.

[0018] In an alternative embodiment, the adaptive controller 150 is implemented as a model reference adaptive controller (MRAC), wherein a reference model defines a desired closed-loop response of patient work of breathing to changes in pressure support, and adaptive laws for controller parameters θ(k) are derived using Lyapunov stability theory such that a Lyapunov function candidate:

$$V(k) = \tilde{\theta}(k)^T \Gamma^{-1} \tilde{\theta}(k)$$

(wherein θ̃(k) is the parameter estimation error and Γ is a positive-definite adaptation gain matrix) is non-increasing along system trajectories, thereby guaranteeing asymptotic or practical stability of the closed-loop adaptive system.

### Stability Preservation Mechanisms

[0019] To further preserve closed-loop stability, the ventilator system 100 may incorporate one or more of the following mechanisms, singly or in combination:

(a) **Rate limiting**: constraining the maximum breath-to-breath change in pressure support, ΔP_support, to a predetermined maximum value ΔP_max, so as to prevent abrupt transitions that could induce patient-ventilator asynchrony or oscillatory control behavior;

(b) **Dead-band logic**: suppressing controller adjustment when the error e(k) falls within a predetermined dead-band threshold, so as to prevent controller "hunting" in response to sensor noise or breath-to-breath physiological variability;

(c) **Estimator confidence weighting**: modulating the adaptive controller's responsiveness to WOB_est(k) based upon a confidence metric or covariance estimate output by the work of breathing estimator 140, such that low-confidence estimates result in reduced or suspended controller adaptation;

(d) **Multi-breath averaging or filtering**: applying a moving average, exponential smoothing, or Kalman filter to WOB_est(k) prior to input into the adaptive controller 150, so as to reduce the influence of breath-to-breath variability on control decisions;

(e) **Fallback safety mode**: reverting to a fixed, clinician-set pressure support level upon detection of estimator divergence, sensor fault, or controller instability, as determined by a supervisory monitoring module 180 configured to monitor one or more stability indicators, including but not limited to rate of change of P_support(k), persistent sign of e(k) over a predetermined number of breaths, or divergence of estimated patient mechanics parameters from physiologically plausible bounds.

# Patient Adaptation Module for Real-Time Ventilator Control

## Overview

The patient adaptation module is a core subsystem within a closed-loop mechanical ventilation controller that continuously estimates patient-specific respiratory parameters and adjusts ventilator control gains to maintain optimal ventilatory support as patient physiology changes over time.

## System Architecture

### 1. Respiratory System Model

The module employs a parametric model of the coupled ventilator-patient system, typically based on the single-compartment lung model:

```
P(t) = R · Q̇(t) + E · V(t) + P₀
```

Where:
- **P(t)** — airway pressure
- **Q̇(t)** — airflow rate
- **V(t)** — lung volume (integrated flow)
- **R** — airway resistance
- **E** — respiratory system elastance (1/compliance)
- **P₀** — baseline/PEEP pressure offset

More sophisticated implementations may incorporate:
- Second-order models capturing viscoelastic (stress-relaxation) behavior
- Nonlinear elastance terms for volume-dependent compliance
- Patient effort estimation (Pmus) for spontaneous breathing modes

### 2. Parameter Estimation Engine

**Recursive Estimation Algorithm**
The module fits model parameters using online estimation techniques suited for real-time, breath-to-breath adaptation:

- **Recursive Least Squares (RLS)** with forgetting factor λ to weight recent data more heavily, accommodating time-varying dynamics
- **Kalman Filtering / Extended Kalman Filter (EKF)** for state and parameter estimation under measurement noise, providing uncertainty bounds on R and E estimates
- **Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE)** batch methods run periodically (e.g., every N breaths) for higher-accuracy recalibration

**Signal Processing Pipeline**
```
Sensor Data (P, Q̇) → Anti-aliasing Filter → Artifact Rejection 
    → Breath Segmentation → Parameter Estimator → Confidence Scoring
```

Artifact rejection handles:
- Patient coughing/movement
- Circuit leaks
- Secretions affecting resistance readings

### 3. Adaptation Logic

**Update Triggering**
- Estimates updated every breath cycle or at fixed intervals (e.g., 5–10 breaths)
- Statistical tests (e.g., residual sum of squares, parameter covariance thresholds) gate whether an update is accepted, preventing noise-driven instability

**Controller Parameter Mapping**
Estimated R and E values feed into the primary ventilator controller (e.g., PID, model predictive control, or adaptive/gain-scheduled control) via:

| Estimated Parameter | Controller Adjustment |
|---|---|
| Increased R | Adjust flow trigger sensitivity, modify pressure ramp slope |
| Increased E (↓ compliance) | Increase pressure gain to maintain target Vt |
| Decreased E | Reduce pressure gain to prevent volutrauma |

### 4. Safety and Stability Safeguards

- **Rate limiting**: Bounds on how quickly controller gains can change per update cycle
- **Parameter bounds**: Physiologically plausible limits on R, E (clamping/saturation)
- **Fallback mode**: Reversion to conservative default parameters if estimation confidence drops or model fit residuals exceed threshold
- **Persistence checks**: Requiring N consecutive consistent estimates before committing to a controller update (hysteresis)

## Data Flow Summary

```
┌─────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌───────────────┐
│  Ventilator  │───▶│  Parameter   │───▶│  Confidence/   │
│  Sensors     │    │  Estimator   │    │  Validity Gate │
│  (P, Q, V)   │    │  (RLS/EKF)   │    │                │
└─────────────┘    └──────────────┘    └───────┬───────┘
                                                 │
                                                 ▼
┌─────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌───────────────┐
│  Patient     │◀───│  Adaptive    │◀───│  Gain          │
│  Airway      │    │  Controller  │    │  Scheduler     │
└─────────────┘    └──────────────┘    └───────────────┘
```

## Performance Considerations

- **Convergence time**: Typically must settle within 3–5 breaths after a physiological change to remain clinically responsive
- **Robustness**: Must tolerate sensor noise, leaks, and asynchrony (patient-ventilator dyssynchrony) without erroneous adaptation
- **Computational constraints**: Algorithms designed for deterministic execution on embedded real-time hardware (typically <10ms per breath cycle for estimation update)

## Clinical Rationale

Patient respiratory mechanics (R, E) evolve due to disease progression, secretion accumulation, positioning changes, or sedation depth. Static controller tuning risks under- or over-ventilation as these parameters drift. Real-time adaptation enables the ventilator to maintain target tidal volume, pressure limits, and synchrony without requiring constant manual clinician intervention, while logging parameter trends to support clinical decision-making.

# Invention Disclosure: Self-Tuning Pressure Support Ventilation System

**Title:** Adaptive Pressure Support Ventilator with Work-of-Breathing Feedback Control

**Summary of Invention:**

This disclosure describes a self-tuning ventilator system that automatically adjusts pressure support (PS) levels using closed-loop feedback derived from the patient's measured work of breathing (WOB) or power of breathing (POB), rather than relying on static, clinician-set pressure values. The system continuously estimates patient respiratory effort in real time by analyzing flow, volume, and airway pressure waveforms to calculate WOB/POB per breath or over a rolling window. This measured value is compared against a clinician-defined or algorithmically-derived target WOB/POB, generating an error signal representative of over-assistance or under-assistance. A control algorithm—implemented as a PID, adaptive, or model-predictive controller—uses this error signal to incrementally titrate the delivered pressure support level, increasing PS when measured effort exceeds the target (indicating patient overexertion) and decreasing PS when effort falls below target (indicating excessive ventilator assistance and risk of muscle disuse atrophy). The controller operates within clinician-defined safety bounds (minimum/maximum PS limits, rate-of-change constraints) and incorporates breath-to-breath smoothing to prevent oscillation or hunting. Novel aspects include: (1) real-time WOB/POB estimation using non-invasive signals (airway pressure, flow, and estimated muscle pressure via reverse-triggering or resistance/compliance modeling) without requiring esophageal balloon catheters; (2) a tunable target-setting mechanism allowing clinicians to specify desired effort ranges based on weaning goals or diaphragm-protective ventilation strategies; and (3) an adaptive learning component that adjusts controller gain based on patient-specific respiratory mechanics trends over time. This approach aims to maintain patient effort within a physiologically appropriate range automatically, reducing clinician workload, minimizing ventilator asynchrony, and supporting lung- and diaphragm-protective ventilation protocols during weaning.
